analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security checks and pays for it with new taxes on income above $250,000 and on investment gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, sent to subcommittees two days later, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits for everyone — about a 22% boost for new beneficiaries, larger annual cost-of-living increases pegged to an inflation index for seniors, a higher minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, and benefits for student children of disabled or deceased workers until age 22. To pay for it, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to all income above $250,000 a year (the current cap is $147,000), extend that tax to self-employment and certain business income above the threshold, and raise the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%. It would also merge the separate retirement and disability trust funds into one Social Security Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — essentially every retiree, disabled worker, and survivor — plus low-earning workers who would get a guaranteed minimum benefit near the poverty line, and student children of deceased or disabled workers who would keep benefits through college. The financing comes from high earners, self-employed professionals, and investors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and low earners

how_it_helps.text: It raises every beneficiary's benefit by boosting the 'bend point' formula factor from 90% to 95% and adding a 22% increase to the base benefit amount for anyone becoming eligible after 2022.

It switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment from the general Consumer Price Index to the CPI for Elderly Consumers, an index tracking what retirees actually buy (mainly housing and medical care), which typically rises faster.

It creates a new minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline that rises with years worked, guaranteeing lifetime low earners — especially people in low-wage and caregiving jobs — a benefit well above today's minimum.
It lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers keep receiving benefits until age 22 while a full-time student, instead of cutting them off at 18.

analysis.who_pays: High earners: everyone earning above $250,000 a year would pay Social Security payroll tax on the excess for the first time, including self-employment income, and investment income would be taxed at 16.2% instead of 3.8% — falling almost entirely on high-income households and business owners.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on high earners, not just their wages: it applies Social Security payroll tax to income above $250,000 and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2%, including on active business income — a large tax increase on professionals, business owners, and investors that critics would call a drag on work and investment.

Employers pay half of the new payroll tax on wages over $250,000, and some economists would note that employer payroll taxes are ultimately borne partly by workers in the form of lower pay — though this falls only on high-wage workplaces.

Using CPI-E for cost-of-living adjustments and recomputing every past beneficiary's benefit permanently raises program costs well beyond current law, which is the point of the bill but represents a large permanent federal commitment that critics argue should be paid for with a broader base of taxes rather than a narrow set of high-income and investment taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to current and future retirees — higher checks, an inflation index that matches what seniors actually buy, and a poverty-level minimum benefit — is large and directly funded by the people asked to pay. The cost is a substantial tax increase on high earners, self-employed professionals, and investors, which could modestly reduce returns on savings and could face arguments about whether taxing investment income at 16.2% affects retirement savings more broadly. The core trade is explicit: benefits up, taxes on the affluent up. The bill's weakness is political, not design: it died without any hearing or committee action, so it received no scrutiny or refinement, and its fiscal assumptions were never independently examined in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and it never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Social Security Expansion Act on June 9, 2022, with 25 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Transportation and Infrastructure committees on the day it was introduced.
Two days later it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security and the Transportation subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and investors keep the current tax treatment of their income; payroll taxes above $250,000 and the 3.8% investment tax rate remain unchanged. Social Security's long-term financing gap remains unsolved, which also preserves the arguments of those who want to address it by cutting benefits or raising the retirement age instead.

for.name: 25 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, McGovern, Raskin, and Tlaib.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its subcommittee referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was held.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the remaining seven months of the Congress.

against.name: 0 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No senator cosponsored the bill, making any Senate path contingent on a House vote that never came.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, though the bill's actual death was by committee inaction rather than a party-line vote.

industries.note: They would pay Social Security tax on earnings above $250,000 (currently wages above roughly $147,000 are taxed and everything above is exempt) and the self-employed would owe the matching share on the same earnings. The bill is aimed directly at ending the cap's benefit for the highest earners.

The net investment income tax would jump from 3.8% to 16.2% and apply to active business income it currently exempts, sharply raising the tax on capital gains and investment returns for high-income households.
Not an industry but the main constituency: every current and future beneficiary gets a roughly 22% benefit increase, higher COLAs, and a poverty-level minimum — paid for by the tax increases above.
